title: History’s lesson for taxing wealth today
gist: Using a new century-plus annual wealth series built from U.S. General Property Tax records, the authors argue direct taxation of wealth stocks at market value is administratively feasible, that the assessed-versus-market-value gap is the central failure mode, and that comprehensive wealth statistics are a high-return public good especially for developing countries where property taxes are the most underused fiscal tool.

insights.claim: The authors built the first comprehensive high-frequency annual U.S. wealth series spanning more than a century from General Property Tax records, a tax that from 1800 to the Great Depression aspired to cover all private property including land, financial assets, livestock, and before emancipation, enslaved people.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: A newly reconstructed long-run wealth dataset gives empirical grounding to modern wealth-tax debates that usually lack historical evidence.
insights.quote: we build the first comprehensive, high-frequency annual wealth series spanning more than one hundred years

insights.claim: The General Property Tax averaged 4 percent of GDP over 1850-1940, financing U.S. governments almost entirely before federal income taxation was established in 1913.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Wealth taxation historically raised substantial revenue at scale, countering the claim that it cannot be a serious fiscal base.

insights.claim: Income-based tax systems structurally understate the economic power of the ultra-rich because capital gains go unrealized, business income is deferred, and much wealth sits in assets like real estate and private equity that generate no reportable income.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: A direct tax on the stock of wealth, assessed near market value, sidesteps the income-flow blind spot that lets top wealth escape measurement.
insights.quote: tax records only capture income flows and not economic capacity of the richest individuals.

insights.claim: U.S. private wealth grew from roughly three times GDP in 1800 to five times by the eve of World War I, collapsed to an all-time low of 195 percent of GDP at the end of the Civil War, and peaked at 580 percent in 1932 as output fell faster than asset values.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The wealth-to-GDP ratio can spike for bad reasons (output collapse), so today's above-5x reading after decades of asset-price growth should not be read naively.
insights.quote: The all-time peak came in 1932, in the depths of the Great Depression: at 580 per cent of GDP

insights.claim: Today U.S. private wealth is again above five times GDP after four decades of asset-price growth near all-time highs.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Current wealth concentration rivals the pre-WWI peak, making the historical taxation lessons directly applicable now.
insights.quote: Today, private wealth is again above five times GDP after four decades of asset-price growth close to all time-highs.

themes.theme: The assessment gap is the failure mode

insights.claim: The U.S. national average property assessment fell from about 83 percent of market value in 1850 to roughly 40 percent by the early twentieth century, as often-elected untrained local assessors undervalued property.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The widening assessed-market gap eroded revenue and ultimately undermined the wealth tax, identifying valuation quality as the make-or-break variable.
insights.quote: fell from about 83 per cent in 1850 to roughly 40 per cent by the early twentieth century

insights.claim: Under-valuation can be regressive: if costly properties are assessed at a lower share of value than cheaper ones, the effective tax rate on the wealthy is lower.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Poor assessment does not just cut revenue, it flips a wealth tax regressive, a live risk in the US, UK and developing countries today.

insights.claim: Accurate valuation requires dedicated infrastructure: the nineteenth-century Census Bureau sent agents into the field, surveyed thousands of experts, and checked assessments against sale prices.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Without independent valuation investment, a wealth tax base is only as good as local assessors allow, usually too low.
insights.quote: Without that infrastructure, the base is whatever assessors say, usually too low for the assets of the wealthy.

insights.claim: Comprehensive decennial Census wealth publications documented property values, exemptions, and assessment practices in every state, letting governments track wealth and hold assessors accountable, a precondition for the tax rather than a by-product.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The authors back current OECD/EU calls for national wealth registers; the cost of not collecting data is not knowing how wealth is distributed or who pays their share.
insights.quote: the cost of not collecting the data is being unable to know how wealth is distributed, how fast it grows, and who pays their fair share.

insights.claim: The wealthiest 10 percent of U.S. counties held around 70 percent of total property by 1930, and rank-rank correlations between county wealth in 1870 and 1930 stayed above 0.6, so wealthy places stayed wealthy for sixty years.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Spatial wealth inequality is far more persistent than income inequality, so income convergence can mask stubborn stock inequality.
insights.quote: the wealthiest 10 per cent of counties held around 70 per cent of total US property by 1930

insights.claim: U.S. counties with wealth more concentrated in the top decile in 1870 grew significantly more slowly over the next sixty years even after controls, with lower education accumulation as a key channel.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Evidence that wealth concentration is a long-run drag on prosperity via human-capital underinvestment strengthens the growth case for wealth taxation.
insights.quote: Counties with wealth more concentrated in the top decile in 1870 grew significantly more slowly over the next sixty years

insights.claim: Property taxes raise only around 0.1 percent of GDP in emerging Asia and Africa, making them the most under-utilized tax in developing countries, constrained by measurement problems rather than tax rates.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Investing in valuation and cadastral infrastructure is a precondition for domestic revenue mobilization, not a luxury for after countries grow rich.
insights.quote: property taxes raise only around 0.1 per cent of GDP in emerging Asia and Africa
